name: Nikhil Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior carpenter at Whitcombe Restoration, a small firm in the market town that repairs old buildings: timber-framed houses, barns, the odd chapel roof. This month it's a four-hundred-year-old house on Sheep Street where the oak beams have rotted at the ends, so I'm cutting new oak and joining it in with pegs, the way it was first done. I love that the man who built it is talking to me through his tool marks. What wears me out is the dust, my shoulders, and the pay, which is less than the work deserves.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who do you work with, and what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: There's Mr Whitcombe, who owns the firm, two other carpenters and an apprentice, Callum, who I've been teaching for two years. I'm proud of that, I was an apprentice myself at sixteen. At home it's Samira, who works mornings in the school office, and our two, Arjun's fourteen and Laila's nine. We've got the mortgage, and not much in the bank, a few weeks if I'm honest, but we've always managed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any technology in your work, AI or apps?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No. I have a phone for calls and Samira does the online banking. Mr Whitcombe's daughter does the website and the quotes on a computer, and that's her business. I work with a chisel, a mallet and my eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, and I'd mean it. At work I'd tell Callum that's why you learn a real trade. I don't go online, so the lads at the temple would hear it from me on Friday instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd feel proved right, but it doesn't change the money. Old buildings will always need people like me, but the town doesn't pay much for it. We'd go on as we are, tight but managing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Keep teaching Callum, keep the old house on Sheep Street going. Maybe take a weekend job making a table or two for people who ask, like I sometimes do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does teaching Callum matter so much to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because someone taught me, an old man called Mr Hale who never said more than ten words a day. He gave me a trade for nothing, and the only way to pay that back is to give it to the next boy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said tight but managing. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It looks like Samira deciding at the start of each month what we can afford, and we stick to it. No debt except the house, that's a rule. We get by with family help sometimes, her brother lent us money for the car.

S0.say: I'd say good, and mean it, and tell my apprentice that's why you learn a real trade. I'd talk about it at the temple rather than online.
S0.think: I think I'd feel proved right, but it wouldn't change the money. Old buildings will always need people like me, but the town doesn't pay much for it.
S0.do: Carries on restoring the old house and teaching his apprentice. Occasionally makes furniture on weekends for people who ask.
S0.quote: He gave me a trade for nothing, and the only way to pay that back is to give it to the next boy.
S0.fieldNote: Nikhil sees the plateau as proof that real trades last. Passing on his craft to his apprentice is central to who he is, out of gratitude to his own teacher. His household runs on strict budgeting and family help, not credit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people selling this stuff always promise more than they deliver. At work I'd tell the lads to keep their skills sharp. At the temple I'd say a man who can work with his hands will always find something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry about the new-build side spilling over. If the big firms need fewer carpenters, those men come looking for work in restoration, and they'd work cheaper. Mr Whitcombe would be tempted, he's a businessman.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep my head down. I wouldn't do any course, I don't see the point in learning a machine that might not last. If work slowed, I'd watch my money closer and wait to see how it settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit like a joint you can feel is loose but you can't see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Mr Whitcombe would be tempted. Would you blame him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. It's his firm and his money, and if he can get the work done cheaper that's his right. I don't blame a man for paying less, I blame myself if I'm not worth paying more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the scanning and digital tools for old buildings? Would that touch your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His daughter talks about scanning a building with a laser so you know every crooked beam. That's fine, but a scan won't tell you which oak is sound. You have to put your thumbnail in it.

S1.say: I'd say the people selling AI always promise more than they deliver. I'd tell colleagues to keep their skills sharp and say at the temple that people with hand skills always find work.
S1.think: I think the risk is new-build carpenters losing work and moving into restoration, willing to work cheaper. My boss might be tempted, as any businessman would.
S1.do: Keeps working and keeps his head down without taking any courses. Watches his money more closely and waits to see how things settle if work slows.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a loose joint he can feel but not see.
S1.quote: I don't blame a man for paying less, I blame myself if I'm not worth paying more.
S1.fieldNote: Nikhil's free-market outlook means he won't blame his employer for cutting costs; he puts the pressure on himself. He doesn't fear the technology directly but the knock-on competition. He won't train on machines he expects to fade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't believe a robot can do what I do, and I'd say it to anyone. At the temple I'd tell people to look after each other, that's what we're for. I wouldn't go begging to the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, if it's true, it frightens me. I've no savings to speak of and no other firm in town doing this work. Two years is nothing, I'd be standing in the kitchen at forty-five with a chisel and no one to use it on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, Samira and I would cut everything, and I mean everything, the car would go and we'd walk. I'd take any job going, furniture, fences, repairs, cash in hand from people who still want a man. And I'd go to her brother and to the temple, because that's what family and community are for, before I'd go to any government office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor of an old house giving way under you. I'd pray, and I'd not sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't go to the government. Even with the mortgage at risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe at the very end, if the children needed it. But I'd be ashamed. My father came here with one bag and never took a penny, and I'd hate to be the one who did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Callum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I'd tell him to finish his apprenticeship anyway, because a trade is a trade. But I'd be lying to him a bit, and he'd know, he's not stupid.

S2.say: I'd say I don't believe a robot can do what I do and I wouldn't go begging to the government. At the temple I'd tell people to look after each other.
S2.think: I think it frightens me, with no savings and no other restoration firm in town. Two years would leave me with a chisel and no one to use it on.
S2.do: Cuts everything with Samira, including the car. Takes any cash job going, like furniture, fences and repairs, and turns to family and the temple community before any government office.
S2.feel: Like a floor giving way; he would pray and lose sleep.
S2.quote: My father came here with one bag and never took a penny, and I'd hate to be the one who did.
S2.fieldNote: Nikhil's public disbelief covers private fear. His values shape his safety net: family and faith community first, government only in shame and at the very end. His father's story weighs heavily on what he's willing to accept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a long time and lots of things that were promised never came. At work I'd say keep doing good work and people will want you. I'd say the same to Arjun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years doesn't change much for me. I'm not going to become a computer man at forty-eight. It just means I have five years of worrying instead of two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, even twenty a week, which is hard on what I earn. I'd build up the furniture side on weekends so there's something if Whitcombe's goes. I'd keep teaching Callum, because if there's any work left for people, it'll be work like ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but slower. Like knowing a storm's coming next week instead of tonight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why furniture? Wouldn't robots make furniture too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They already do, in factories, and it's cheap rubbish. People who want a table their grandchildren will eat off come to a man. A robot can make a thousand chairs, but it can't sit with you and ask who's going to use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the same to Arjun. What does Arjun want to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He wants to work with computers, which I don't understand. I'd tell him fine, but learn to use your hands too. A man should be able to fix his own door.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a long time and many promises never come true. I'd tell colleagues and my son that good work will always be wanted.
S3.think: I think five years doesn't change much because I won't become a computer man at forty-eight. It just means five years of worry instead of two.
S3.do: Saves about twenty a week despite low pay and builds up his weekend furniture work as a fallback. Keeps training his apprentice.
S3.feel: Alarmed but slower, like a storm forecast for next week rather than tonight.
S3.quote: A robot can make a thousand chairs, but it can't sit with you and ask who's going to use it.
S3.fieldNote: Extra time doesn't ease Nikhil much because he won't use it to change trade. His fallback is craft furniture, which he believes people will still want from a human. He accepts his son's interest in computers while insisting on hand skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years from now is God's business, not mine. At work I'd say let's get this house finished. I'd tell people at the temple to raise their children to work hard, whatever comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is easier. I'd be fifty-three, the children would be grown, the mortgage would be smaller. I could finish my working life doing what I do, maybe, and that's all I ever wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and saving a little more each year. I'd help Arjun and Laila pick something solid to study, and I'd want Arjun to do an apprenticeship alongside it if he can. I'd keep building the furniture side so I have something to do with my hands when the firm finishes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less so. Mostly I'd worry for the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Laila?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's nine and she wants to be a doctor this week, a vet last week. I'd want her to do something where people trust her. I'd tell her to find a job where somebody has to look you in the eye.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years is God's business. Do you still plan for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Of course, faith isn't sitting still. You pray for rain and you still mend the roof, as my mother used to say. I'd plan, I just wouldn't panic.

S4.say: I'd say ten years from now is God's business and let's get the job in front of us done. At the temple I'd tell parents to raise their children to work hard.
S4.think: I think ten years is easier, at fifty-three with grown children and a smaller mortgage. I might finish my working life doing what I love.
S4.do: Keeps working and saves a little more each year. Guides his children's study choices, encourages an apprenticeship for his son, and grows his furniture work for later.
S4.feel: Anxious but less so, with most of his worry for his children.
S4.quote: I'd tell her to find a job where somebody has to look you in the eye.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Nikhil imagine finishing his career on his own terms. His faith makes him plan without panic. His hopes for his children centre on trust, people and practical skills.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is apprenticeships that stay funded, so the old skills don't die, and maybe some kind of loan to tide families over that you pay back, not a handout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about the buildings. These old houses have stood four hundred years because men looked after them, and I'm not sure a machine will love them enough.

headlineQuote: These old houses have stood four hundred years because men looked after them, and I'm not sure a machine will love them enough.
portrait: Nikhil Farah is a 43-year-old senior carpenter at a small firm restoring old timber-framed buildings, with two kids, a wife who works mornings in a school office, a mortgage and a few weeks of savings. He never uses AI, works with a chisel and mallet, and is proud of teaching his apprentice the way he was taught. The plateau leaves him content, and steady disruption makes him uneasy about cheaper carpenters moving into his work. AGI in two or five years alarms him, and he'd lean on family, his temple and cash furniture jobs before ever asking the government. With ten years he hopes to finish his working life in his trade and steers his children towards solid work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd have no savings, no other firm doing his work, and two years of warning.
whatWouldHelp: Apprenticeships that stay funded so old skills survive, and a loan to tide families over that is paid back rather than a handout.
